summary: Describes TCP performance problems caused by path asymmetry, as in bandwidth-asymmetric networks and packet radio. Different causes lead to the same result: poor or variable acknowledgment feedback from receiver to sender hurts performance. It surveys the problems and ways to mitigate them.

plainLanguage.summary: If the road one way is fast and the way back is slow, replies get stuck. TCP depends on replies, so it slows down. This note explains that and offers fixes.

questions: how does asymmetry affect tcp performance
does tcp header compression help asymmetric links
subtitle: Why a slow or unreliable return path starves TCP of acknowledgments, and which fixes are worth using.

tldr.problem: On many access networks (cable, satellite, ADSL, packet radio) the path back from receiver to sender is much worse than the forward path, so TCP acknowledgments (ACKs) arrive late, bunched up or not at all.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains how this degrades TCP and surveys mitigations: host changes, header compression, ACK filtering and reconstruction, and smarter scheduling at the slow upstream link. Each one is labelled recommended, experimental or not recommended.
tldr.outcome: A Best Current Practice survey with a summary table. Only a few techniques are recommended as they stand, such as Path MTU discovery, header compression for mild asymmetry, traffic shaping and per-flow queuing.

facts.label: Worked example of k
facts.value: 10 Mbps down, 50 Kbps up, 1000-byte data, 40-byte ACKs gives k = 8

facts.label: Per-flow queuing
facts.value: Widely deployed on links under 2 Mbps

today: RFC 3449 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 69). According to the metadata for this site it has not been obsoleted or updated by another RFC. It is a survey of options as they stood in December 2002, and many of its mitigations are marked experimental there.

sections.title: Terms Used for Asymmetric Paths
sections.content:
The RFC defines its vocabulary first. The forward direction is the direction of the main data transfer and usually has the better capacity, latency and error rate. The reverse direction carries the acknowledgments of that transfer and is typically worse. The upstream link is the bottleneck link on the reverse path; the downstream link is its partner on the forward path.

Three more terms recur. The delayed ACK factor d is how many data segments one ACK covers (at least 1). A stretch ACK covers more than 2 segments (d>2). The normalized bandwidth ratio k is the ratio of forward to return raw bandwidth, divided by the ratio of packet sizes in the two directions.
sections.plainLanguage: The road for the big trucks is the forward direction. The little road for the thank-you notes coming back is the reverse direction, and the notes are the ACKs.

sections.title: Where Asymmetry Comes From
sections.content:
Asymmetry shows up in cable data networks, direct broadcast satellite, VSAT terminals, ADSL and several packet radio networks. The RFC names two root causes.

  • Different capacity. The upstream and downstream links run at different rates or use different technologies. Sharing the upstream with other traffic, such as telephony with reserved capacity, makes it worse.
  • Shared reverse media. In a hub-and-spokes network each node must first ask for upstream bandwidth through a contention MAC protocol. The per-packet overhead can make a short ACK as costly as an MTU-sized data packet.

The two causes differ, but the harm is the same: imperfect and variable ACK feedback to the sender.
sections.plainLanguage: Sometimes the return road is narrow. Sometimes lots of people share one little return road and must ask permission before each trip. Either way, the thank-you notes get stuck.

sections.title: How Asymmetry Hurts TCP
sections.content:
If the upstream buffer is deep enough that ACKs are not dropped, performance depends on k. The RFC's example: a 10 Mbps downstream link and a 50 Kbps upstream link give a capacity ratio of 200; with 1000-byte data packets and 40-byte ACKs the size ratio is 25, so k is 8. Acknowledging more often than once per 8 data packets saturates the upstream link first. ACKs then queue and spread out, so the sender's ACK clocking slows and the congestion window (cwnd) grows more slowly.

If the upstream buffer is small, ACKs are dropped. The sender then sends big bursts, grows cwnd slowly because it counts ACKs, and has weaker Fast Retransmit and Fast Recovery because it may not see enough duplicate ACKs.

MAC interactions add variable delay. On the Ricochet packet radio network, TCP timeouts of 9 to 12 seconds were not uncommon and connections were sometimes idle for 35% of the transfer time. Two-way traffic is worse: large reverse-direction data packets can queue ahead of ACKs, and queued ACKs can be compressed in time (ACK Compression), producing bursts. The RFC notes that losing ACKs is less serious than losing data, because it generally just produces stretch ACKs.
sections.plainLanguage: If the thank-you notes pile up and arrive all at once, the sender either waits too long or sends a big rush of packages. Both are bad for a smooth delivery.

sections.title: Fixes in the End Hosts
sections.content:
Two issues must be handled: manage the capacity of the upstream link, and avoid harm from fewer ACKs. Section 4 covers changes in the end hosts, each ending with a recommendation.

  • Modified delayed ACKs: not recommended. A receiver must follow the standard algorithm of RFC 2581, with d not exceeding 2 and an ACK within 500 ms.
  • Large MSS: use Path MTU discovery (RFC 1191) to take advantage of a large forward MTU. Using a larger MSS with IP fragmentation by routers is not recommended.
  • ACK Congestion Control, Window Prediction Mechanism, cwnd-estimation ACKs: receiver-side schemes that vary d. ACC is experimental; the other two are not recommended in their current form.
  • TCP sender pacing: limits back-to-back bursts. Experimental.
  • Byte counting: grows cwnd by the data acknowledged instead of by the number of ACKs. Unlimited byte counting is not allowed, so it needs a burst-limiting safeguard.
  • Backpressure: limits queued upstream data packets so ACKs are not starved. Experimental.
sections.plainLanguage: The sender and receiver can change their habits, such as sending fewer thank-you notes or sending packages more evenly. Most of these ideas are still being tried out.

sections.title: Fixes Inside the Network
sections.content:
Section 5 covers transparent modifications, so called because the TCP sender and receiver need not know about them. They need to see unencrypted IP and TCP headers and tell flows apart. They fall into four types.

  • Type 0, header compression: TCP header compression (RFC 1144) shrinks ACKs and is recommended for low-to-medium asymmetry (for example k<10). It does not help with IP or TCP options, tunnels or encrypted traffic, and loses efficiency when packets are lost. Robust header compression (ROHC) is discussed as promising.
  • Type 1, bandwidth management: ACK Filtering removes older queued ACKs of the same connection but keeps ACKs with data or flags such as SYN, RST, URG or FIN. ACK Decimation uses per-flow queues and a drop policy; ACK Filtering is preferred where possible. Both can create stretch ACKs and bursts.
  • Type 2, handling infrequent ACKs: ACK Reconstruction regenerates missing ACKs after the upstream link, up to (delta/ackthresh) - 2 of them. ACK Compaction and Companding add a prefix recording what was removed. Generic Traffic Shaping on the forward path smooths bursts and is recommended alongside Type 1 schemes.
  • Type 3, link scheduling: per-flow queuing is recommended and widely deployed on links under 2 Mbps. ACKs-first scheduling is experimental and not recommended yet, because it could starve data packets.
sections.plainLanguage: Helpers along the road can shrink the notes, throw away duplicate notes, put back notes that were removed, or let notes skip the line. Some helpers are safe to use now and some are still experiments.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says its recommendations do not affect the integrity of TCP or introduce new security issues for TCP or its applications. IPsec does limit what is possible. With ESP encryption, the TCP header cannot be read or changed, which rules out header compression, ACK Filtering, ACK Reconstruction and ACK Compaction. With AH the header can be read but not modified, which rules out generating new packets, as ACK Reconstruction does.

Type 2 schemes carry a denial-of-service risk. A reconstructor can be abused as a packet amplifier if a third party injects stretch ACKs. The RFC says to verify the tunnel end point, make sure applications cannot falsely inject packets that expand, and consider a rate limit and a bound on d.
sections.plainLanguage: If the notes are locked in sealed envelopes, helpers cannot read them or change them. A helper that makes extra notes could also be tricked into making far too many.

sections.title: Summary of Recommendations
sections.content:
The RFC closes with two tables that label every technique as recommended (REC), not recommended (NOT REC) or experimental (EXP). Experimental techniques need more operational experience before they can be recommended for the public Internet. Some of the table entries carry footnotes; for example, header compression may degrade TCP at high asymmetry but is not considered harmful to the Internet.

Overall, the document treats asymmetry as an ACK-feedback problem with two goals: keep the upstream link from being swamped by ACKs, and keep the sender's ACK-driven self-clocking intact when ACKs become rare.
sections.plainLanguage: At the end there is a report card. Each idea gets a label: good to use, still an experiment, or please do not use yet.
